pages.text: An HF station works without a ground, but a good one makes it $(thing)quieter$(): most of the local hash from redstone and nearby lightning rides in on the coax shield, and a ground drains it off, along with some of the band noise.$(br2)A ground is $(item)ground rods$() driven into the earth, bonded to the station with $(item)ground wire$() (green wire). No other colour bonds a rod.

pages.title: Where to bond
pages.text: Run ground wire from a ground rod to the radio itself, or better, to the $(l:radiocraft:safety/lightning#arrestor)lightning arrestor$(/l)'s ground lug where the coax comes in. A grounded arrestor grounds every radio on its coax, as professional sites do it (single point grounding), and it needs that ground to stop every strike.

pages.title: A good ground
pages.text: It depends on the soil, the depth and the wet. $(thing)Mud and damp clay$() are best, then ordinary dirt. $(thing)Sand, gravel, rock and frozen ground$() are poor: go deeper or drive more rods. Stack rods down a hole and fill the soil back round them; bond rods together for more. Rain, water nearby and a wet biome all help.$(br2)Use a rod to have its ground measured.

pages.title: Ground faults
pages.text: A ground run carries $(thing)no power$(). A battery, solar panel or charge controller on the same green wire as a rod is a ground fault: the rod sparks and the batteries drain into the earth. Keep power on other wire.
Copper-clad steel, like the real thing.
